name: MemLLM

paper.title: MemLLM: Finetuning LLMs to Use Explicit Read-Write Memory

construction.unit: relation triple (subject, relation, object) over 96 Wikidata relation types
construction.kept_as: extracted triples; entity and relation names as text plus Contriever vectors
construction.processing: finetuned write model reads each sentence with its preceding sentences and emits a MEM_WRITE call listing the triples in that sentence

organization.structure: triple store: a Triples table of (subject id, relation id, object id) linked to Entities and Relations tables
organization.stores: Triple Memory; Entities (name, vector); Relations (name, vector)
organization.index: Contriever vectors of entity and relation names (HNSW in code); each (s, r, o) stored once

management.operations: insert; identical triples and names are stored once
management.conflicts: knowledge-editing runs only: a new triple with the same entity and relation replaces the old one (§4.3)

retrieval.query: the read model decides where to read and writes queries (s, r, ?) or (?, r, o) in a MEM_READ call
retrieval.candidates: entities and relations whose name vectors are close to the query's (cosine thresholds)
retrieval.selection: triples joining a candidate entity and relation whose mean similarity passes a threshold; the other entity's name is returned
retrieval.budget: at most 30 entity names per call (paper: drop the call above 30; code: keep 30 names taken from an unordered set, i.e. unranked)

use.context: returned entity names appended inline after the call; the call is deleted when the next one starts
use.reasoning: the model keeps decoding (language modeling, or a 5-shot QA answer in editing)

classify.note: Memory is an entity-relation triple store; the model writes the query, but the matching is a fixed similarity-threshold rule over name vectors (no graph walk, no reranker). Replacement of old triples happens only in the knowledge-editing experiment.

stages.ingestion: Text is split into sentences; each sentence is given to the write model as the focus sentence, bracketed by tags, after the preceding sentences (up to 24 in the Wikipedia indexing script).
stages.construction: A LoRA-finetuned Mistral-7B emits ({MEM_WRITE--> s»r»o; ...}) with the triples stated in the focus sentence, using late stopping so it does not close the list too early.
stages.organization: Triples go into a Triples table that points to separate Entities and Relations tables; names are stored once as text with a Contriever vector.
stages.update: Identical triples are stored once. In the knowledge-editing run a new triple with the same entity and relation as an old one replaces it.
stages.retrieval: While generating, the read model emits ({MEM_READ( with one to a few (s, r, ?) or (?, r, o) queries; candidate entities and relations are found by cosine similarity of name vectors, matching triples are joined, and up to 30 entity names are returned.
stages.answer: The returned names are appended after '-->' and the model continues; the call is removed when the model starts a new one, or right away if nothing came back.
stages.learning: Two LoRA adapters on Mistral-7B are finetuned with the language-modeling loss on API data built from Re-DocRED, distant-supervised DocRED (filtered with Mixtral) and counterfactual Re-DocRED variants; read data is built against a memory filled by the trained write model.

summary: An LLM finetuned to call an explicit triple-store memory: a write model extracts (subject, relation, object) triples sentence by sentence, and a read model inserts MEM_READ queries mid-generation whose matched entity names are appended to the text.

The list guess 'TMLR 2025 journal' is confirmed from the arXiv v3 PDF; the OpenReview page itself sat behind a browser check and was not read. DESIGN: §3.1 (memory structure, query rule), §3.2 (API, inference), §3.3 (training data), §4.1 (setup), App. A (late stopping), App. B (ambiguous queries), App. D (hyperparameters). Trigger is 'other': writing runs once per sentence of any input text, not per dialogue turn. Retrieval control is learned-sft because the finetuned model decides where to read and what to ask; the match itself is a fixed rule.

sources.code_note: Commit f786ae30 (2024-08-13, 'Added codes') is the only commit with code; all later history is README edits before it, and the repo has not changed since, while paper v3 is from 2025-04. It is taken as the evaluation code. Released scripts have placeholder paths (model dirs, memory server URI), so exact run settings can only be read from the constants in the eval scripts.

headline: Memory is a database of (subject, relation, object) triples that the model itself writes and queries through special text calls it learned by finetuning.
What comes back is only a list of entity names, not the triples: the model must infer from its own query what each name answers.
In the perplexity evaluation, reads happen only at positions fixed by the evaluation data (before target entities); the model's choice enters as the probability of opening a call there.

write.how: nltk sentence split; each sentence becomes the focus, preceded by earlier sentences as context

write model emits ({MEM_WRITE--> s»r»o; ...}); greedy with late stopping: when the close token wins, remember the cut point and keep decoding until the score has not improved 5 times, then cut at the best point
write.out: an empty list is allowed (trained on sentences without relations)

write.how: look up names; embed and insert new entity and relation names; insert triples with INSERT OR IGNORE so duplicates are dropped

read.how: the read model emits '({' while generating; the model learned where from training data that places a read just before a target entity
model generates MEM_READ(s»r»; »r»o; ...)--> ; training data holds up to 3 queries per call
read.src: paper §3.2, Alg. 1 L27; code memllm.py L252-L288

read.scores: query entity name and query relation name vs stored names
read.how: HNSW search on Contriever vectors; keep entities within distance 0.15 (of the nearest 300) and relations within 0.15 (of the nearest 25)
read.src: paper §3.1, App. D; code memory_controller_v3.py L153-L157, evaluate_v4_mistral.py L54-L55

read.how: for each entity x relation pair with mean distance < 0.1, fetch matching triples by SQL; if any exact name match exists (distance < 0.001), keep only those
collect the other entity's name from every triple, dedupe with a Python set and keep 30 of them (set order, so no ranking); if none, drop the call and continue without memory

answer_context.sees: the text so far plus the latest call with up to 30 entity names
excludes: the matched triples and their relations
the source sentences of the facts
includes: entity names returned by the latest read
answer_context.note: An empty result or a new '({' removes the call from the context.

compression.what: stored records vs one proposition per fact
compression.basis: Full Wikipedia: 111M extracted triples need about 21M entity/relation rows with vectors, versus 111M embedded propositions for an equivalent RAG store (§4.2, Fig. 4).

paper_vs_code.paper: 1000 sequential edits, compared with WISE's numbers

open_questions: Rows 1-3 of Table 2 differ in both memory size and whether the memory holds facts from the evaluated documents themselves, so the small gap does not isolate scaling.

The editing comparison mixes protocols: baselines copied from WISE are scored after all 1000 edits with token-level accuracy, MemLLM by answer containment in a script that scores each edit right after writing it.

discussion.takeaway: Finetuning an LLM to write and query an explicit triple store through text API calls lowers perplexity on entities that memory can supply, and the same memory handles 1000 sequential knowledge edits better than the parametric editors it is compared with.

claims.claim: Memory reads improve language modeling, mostly on target entities.
claims.evidence: TARGET PPL 2.986 with a full-Wikipedia memory vs 3.510 with memory disabled and 3.550 for Mistral-7B (Table 2, §4.2).

claims.claim: The approach scales with memory size.
claims.evidence: 111M-triple Wikipedia memory is only slightly worse than a memory built from the evaluation documents alone (TARGET 2.986 vs 2.821, Table 2).

claims.claim: Better memory reads and writes would help further.
claims.evidence: Gold queries on gold triples reach TARGET 1.364; own writes with gold positions and queries 1.938 (Table 2 rows 4, 7).

claims.claim: Outperforms knowledge-editing methods on sequential edits.
claims.evidence: ZsRE, 1000 edits, Mistral-7B: AVG 0.84 vs WISE 0.79, GRACE 0.67, DEFER 0.24 (Table 3).

claims.claim: Structured storage is more compact than proposition-level RAG.
claims.evidence: Under 20% of records at 111M facts (§4.2, Fig. 4).

limits: Only the 96 relation types used in training can be extracted and queried.
Relations that follow from several stored triples are neither inferred nor used.
The model does not know what memory lacks: if a fact is missing it falls back on parametric knowledge or hallucinates.
reading: The model only sees returned entity names, not the triples; the paper's own error analysis has cases where the right name came back under the wrong relation and was ignored (§4.3).

In the perplexity code the read positions come from the evaluation data (just before annotated target entities) and the with/without-read outputs are mixed by the probability of '({'; so 'MemLLM chooses where to read' is measured only at those positions (footnote 3; evaluate_v4_mistral.py L120-L176).
Much of the OVERALL gain over Mistral-7B comes from in-domain finetuning alone (5.823 → 4.997 with memory disabled); memory adds 4.997 → 4.905.

The ZsRE baselines are copied from WISE and scored with EasyEdit token accuracy after all 1000 edits; the released MemLLM script scores answer containment and evaluates each edit right after writing it, so Table 3 does not compare like with like.
Code thresholds differ from App. D in both experiments (see paper vs code).
The reliability error breakdown (45 write, 95 read, 63 not used) adds up to 203 of the 216 errors the paper counts; the remaining 13 are not explained (§4.3).

abstract.text: MemLLM gives an LLM an explicit, structured memory it can both write to and read from. Facts are kept as (subject, relation, object) triples in database tables, with entity and relation names embedded for fuzzy matching. Two LoRA adapters on Mistral-7B are finetuned on data built from relation-annotated Wikipedia text: one writes the triples found in each sentence, the other issues memory queries during generation and uses the returned entities. On Re-DocRED the memory lowers perplexity, especially on entities, and on ZsRE it handles 1000 sequential edits better than model-editing baselines.
